{{Short description|Principle in compass and straightedge constructions}}

In [[geometry]], the '''compass equivalence theorem''' is an important statement in [[straightedge and compass construction|compass and straightedge constructions]]. The tool advocated by [[Plato]] in these constructions is a ''divider'' or ''collapsing compass'', that is, a [[compass (drafting)|compass]] that "collapses" whenever it is lifted from a page, so that it may not be directly used to transfer distances. The ''modern compass'' with its fixable aperture can be used to transfer distances directly and so appears to be a more powerful instrument. However, the compass equivalence theorem states that any construction via a "modern compass" may be attained with a collapsing compass. This can be shown by establishing that with a collapsing compass, given a [[circle]] in the plane, it is possible to construct another circle of equal [[radius]], centered at any given point on the plane. This theorem is Proposition II of Book I of [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']]. The [[Mathematical proof|proof]] of this [[theorem]] has had a chequered history.<ref name=Toussaint>{{Cite journal |last=Toussaint |first=Godfried T. |author-link=Godfried Toussaint |date=January 1993 |title=A New Look at Euclid's Second Proposition |url=http://cgm.cs.mcgill.ca/~godfried/teaching/dm-reading-assignments/Euclid-Second-Proposition-Math-Intell.pdf |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=12–24 |doi=10.1007/bf03024252 |issn=0343-6993 | eissn=1866-7414 | publisher = Springer US|s2cid=26811463 }}</ref>

==Construction==
[[File:Euclid2.svg|thumb|300px|Diagram for proof of Euclid I.2]]
The following construction and proof of correctness are given by Euclid in his ''Elements''.<ref>{{cite book  | last = Heath  | first = Thomas L.  | author-link = T. L. Heath  | title = The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements  | edition = 2nd  | orig-year = 1925  | year = 1956  | publisher = Dover Publications  | location = New York  | isbn = 0-486-60088-2  | page = [https://archive.org/details/thirteenbooksofe00eucl/page/244 244]  | url-access = registration  | url = https://archive.org/details/thirteenbooksofe00eucl/page/244  }}</ref> Although there appear to be several cases in Euclid's treatment, depending upon choices made when interpreting ambiguous instructions, they all lead to the same conclusion,<ref name=Toussaint /> and so, specific choices are given below.

Given points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}}, construct a circle centered at {{mvar|A}} with radius the length of {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} (that is, equivalent to the solid green circle, but centered at {{mvar|A}}).
* Draw a circle centered at {{mvar|A}} and passing through {{mvar|B}} and vice versa (the red circles).  They will intersect at point {{mvar|D}} and form the [[equilateral triangle]] {{math|△''ABD''}}.
* Extend {{mvar|{{overline|DB}}}} past {{mvar|B}} and find the intersection of {{mvar|{{overline|DB}}}} and the circle {{math|◯''BC''}}, labeled {{mvar|E}}.
* Create a circle centered at {{mvar|D}} and passing through {{mvar|E}} (the blue circle).
* Extend {{mvar|{{overline|DA}}}} past {{mvar|A}} and find the intersection of {{mvar|{{overline|DA}}}} and the circle {{math|◯''DE''}}, labeled {{mvar|F}}.
* Construct a circle centered at {{mvar|A}} and passing through {{mvar|F}} (the dotted green circle)
* Because {{math|△''ADB''}} is an equilateral triangle, {{math|1={{overline|''DA''}} = {{overline|''DB''}}}}.
* Because {{mvar|E}} and {{mvar|F}} are on a circle around {{mvar|D}}, {{math|1={{overline|''DE''}} = {{overline|''DF''}}}}.
* Therefore, {{math|1={{overline|''AF''}} = {{overline|''BE''}}}}.
* Because {{mvar|E}} is on the circle {{math|◯''BC''}}, {{math|1={{overline|''BE''}} = {{overline|''BC''}}}}.
* Therefore, {{math|1={{overline|''AF''}} = {{overline|''BC''}}}}.

==Alternative construction without straightedge==
It is possible to prove compass equivalence without the use of the straightedge. This justifies the use of "fixed compass" moves (constructing a circle of a given radius at a different location) in proofs of the [[Mohr–Mascheroni theorem]], which states that any construction possible with straightedge and compass can be accomplished with compass alone.

[[File:Compass-equivalence-no-straightedge.png|300px|thumb|Construction without using straightedge]]
Given points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}}, construct a circle centered at {{mvar|A}} with the radius {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}}, using only a collapsing compass and no straightedge.
* Draw a circle centered at {{mvar|A}} and passing through {{mvar|B}} and vice versa (the blue circles). They will intersect at points {{mvar|D}} and {{mvar|D'}}. 
* Draw circles through {{mvar|C}} with centers at {{mvar|D}} and {{mvar|D'}} (the red circles). Label their other intersection {{mvar|E}}.
* Draw a circle (the green circle) with center {{mvar|A}} passing through {{mvar|E}}. This is the required circle.<ref name=Eves>{{citation|first=Howard|last=Eves|title=A survey of Geometry (Vol. I)|year=1963|publisher=Allyn Bacon|page=185}}</ref><ref name=Smart>{{citation|first=James R.|last=Smart|title=Modern Geometries|edition=5th|year=1997|publisher=Brooks/Cole|isbn=0-534-35188-3|page=212}}</ref>

There are several proofs of the correctness of this construction and it is often left as an exercise for the reader.<ref name=Eves /><ref name=Smart /> Here is a modern one using [[Geometric transformation|transformations]].

* The line {{mvar|DD'}} is the [[perpendicular bisector]] of {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}}.  Thus {{mvar|A}} is the [[reflection (geometry)|reflection]] of {{mvar|B}} through line {{mvar|DD'}}.
* By construction, {{mvar|E}} is the reflection of {{mvar|C}} through line {{mvar|DD'}}.
* Since reflection is an [[isometry]], it follows that {{math|1={{overline|''AE''}} = {{overline|''BC''}}}} as desired.
